#### Into the Deep: A Memoir from the Man Who Found Titanic

Robert D. Ballard and Christopher Drew. Washington, DC: National Geographic Partners, 2021. 335 pp. Images. Notes. Index. $30.

Reviewed by Captain Don Walsh, U.S. Navy (Retired)

This memoir is like a personal conversation between author and reader. According to end comments by coauthor Christopher Drew, the book was an effort in which individuals researched and wrote drafts of the chapters—the primary sources of Ballard’s life story are 200 hours of recorded interviews and his extensive personal archive.

A better subtitle could have been “Inside the Life and Mind of an Explorer.” Though the dust jacket states he was the man who found the Titanic, Dr. Robert Ballard is no one-trick pony. Though the Titanic discovery was important, it did not define him. He has had many “lives” as adventurer, distinguished marine geologist, and respected educator. In addition, he has been an extraordinarily effective media celebrity, engaging the lay public with his ocean-related stories.

He is a deliberate rereader who returns to a small set of durable books rather than chasing novelty, and he has a documented system for keeping what he finds: "After I’ve finished a book, I usually put it on my desk for a week or two, let it sit, and then I come back to it.   * His own books used only as evidence of how his reading became his writing, never as recommendations

What we’re still checking
    Farnam Street is a large site full of book summaries, reading lists and guest recommendations, and not every book that appears there is Shane’s personal pick. This page curates a smaller core that traces to his own first-person recommendations, reads his annual reading lists by what he actually says about each book, and distinguishes books he recommended, reread, discussed, or merely encountered.

Books recommended by guests on The Knowledge Project are not treated as Shane’s recommendations. Shane’s own books (The Great Mental Models, Clear Thinking) appear only in the narrative, to show how a reader and curator became an author.

# The Great Mental Models

Volume 1: General Thinking Concepts

by Shane Parrish

Summary by the Atenu Editorial Team · July 27, 2026

Read 13 min

Image: The Great Mental Models cover

## Recommendation

The Great Mental Models, Volume 1 argues that good decisions come less from raw intelligence than from a stocked toolkit of reliable ideas. Shane Parrish borrows the framing from the investor Charlie Munger, who spoke of carrying a broad “latticework of mental models,” chunks of knowledge drawn from many disciplines that can be simplified and applied to understand almost any situation. A mental model, in this telling, is a compression of how something works, a lens you can hold up to a problem. This first volume presents nine such lenses, the general thinking concepts, and shows what each one is and when to reach for it.

The book is written for anyone who has to make hard calls without a clear answer in front of them. A small-business owner deciding whether to expand, a lifelong learner who wants to think more clearly, a diaspora professional weighing a move, a manager reading a confusing situation, a parent teaching a child how to reason: all of them will find tools here. ## Summary

Parrish builds the book as a preface and introduction on why thinking better matters, followed by one chapter per model, with three shorter “supporting ideas” woven in. The introduction, titled “Acquiring Wisdom,” sets the goal: reducing blind spots. If you had perfect information, he writes, you would always choose well, the way you would play a poker hand with every card face up. We cannot remove our blind spots, but we can shrink them, and mental models are how we do it. The chapters that follow are grouped here into four families.

### Why a latticework beats a stack of facts

The organizing image is Munger’s latticework. Most of us learn one discipline deeply and then reach for its tools everywhere, the way, in the old saying, a person with only a hammer sees every problem as a nail. An engineer thinks in systems, a psychologist in incentives, a businessperson in opportunity cost, and each sees only the slice of reality that their training lit up. Parrish retells the parable of blind men and an elephant, each touching one part and declaring the whole to be a snake, a fan, a pillar, a wall. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
